chapter: Paris, the Blackbirds and Noble Sissle
title: Ladnier's weak reading, the Bach 7 mouthpiece and later improvement
summary: Ladnier read poorly but later studied theory and arranged; Briggs explains how the deep Bach 7 mouthpiece hurt him and gave him a shallower one.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: We were talking about Tommy Ladnier.
Yes.
Tommy, in other words, Tommy couldn't read, he didn't have any control of his horn.
No, he didn't have the proper intuition of his horn. He didn't read very, very well. But, in the latter years he studied theory, and harmony, and he started to make arrangements that were not so bad.
Briggs
Really.
Yes. He did two or three arrangements for Sissle. Not bad.
So, he could -- he eventually --
Yes, and as I told you, the mouthpiece that I made him a present of, he played much better the last recording that I heard with Metro. (Zerrol)
Right.

And he made a top D, 'cause he always told me, Tommy, he said to me, things like that I understand, he said, "When I was with Fletcher (He) Anderson's orchestra, one of the arrangements I had to open, and hitting a top D."
He said, "I opened the number with a top D." So, I said to him, "What have you been doing since?" (Laughter).
Well, it wasn't surprising, because he -- I'll tell you, the truth is, he played with a Bach #7.
Briggs
Yes.
That's a hard mouthpiece.
Is it?
Very hard. I played with a #8 for quite some time. And then I changed. I changed and had a mouthpiece made in France with a shallower cup.
Yeh.
That Bach mouthpiece is on a 7 keel.
Of course it was what, too deep?
Too deep.
Very deep cup.
Too deep. Too large and too deep.
Right.
And too deep, it would kill you.
And I made him a present of that mouthpiece and he played much better with it.
Briggs 220
But he played with a 7 and I remember telling him, when he came to Sissle's orchestra, I said, "Tommy, why don't you try to change your mouthpiece?"
And he said, "No, man, this is perfect, I don't have to blow much." And I said, "Yes, if you play up at G above the line." (Laughter).
You have to -- if you go any further -- (Laughter).
Yes.
Well, anyhow, he was a fine --
Well, was he having trouble with booze then too.
No, not at that time, not then. I think he had stopped. He had learned his lesson and the booze had taken care of him before, I think.
Yes.
'Cause most of them, had had (inaudible)
Briggs 221
He'd been sick from it?
Yes.
